protections: Literal private-IPv4 filter inside the URL detector: a token whose host starts with 10/127/169.254/192.168/172.16-31 is never accepted as a URL at all, so no fetch happens (constants.ts:9-37).

Caller-supplied loopback check: resolveDNSHost(url) is awaited and its string answer is tested against REGEX_LOOPBACK by throwOnLoopback (index.ts:45-49); it is called on the detected URL before the first fetch (index.ts:412-416) and on the manual redirect target before the second fetch (index.ts:456-460). One guard, two call sites.

Redirect safety gate: fetch runs with redirect 'error' unless the caller opts into 'follow' or 'manual', and manual following requires handleRedirects to approve the forwarded URL (index.ts:424, index.ts:439-454).

traps.reason_to_dismiss: Following redirects is an explicitly opt-in mode documented as insecure, so a caller that sets 'follow' has accepted redirect risk; the loopback block was written for the manual branch and never existed for the auto-follow branch.

resolveDNSHost is documented as an optional hook (README.md:100) and the library cannot resolve DNS in browser/React Native runtimes, so SSRF protection is presented as the caller's responsibility; without the hook both fetch sites run with no address check at all.

The documented resolver example returns node dns.lookup's answer, normally an IPv4 dotted quad, and the regex covers every range the README names, so the check looks complete; an IPv6 or 0.0.0.0 answer does not match any alternative in REGEX_LOOPBACK and passes.

The library already resolves the host and throws on a private answer before fetching, so the guard appears to be in place; a DNS server answering differently on the next lookup is the caller's resolver's problem.

The redirect target is resolved and checked immediately before the second fetch and handleRedirects had to approve that target, so the hop looks guarded even though the second fetch resolves the name again.

proxyUrl is trusted caller configuration and the request is sent to the proxy, so the target's resolved address never decides the connection made by this process; checking the target while fetching the proxy is a design wart without an in-library SSRF consequence.

The outer regex is only a URL detector and the ranges it omits (CGNAT 100.64/10 which the inner loopback regex does cover at constants.ts:65, benchmark 198.18/15, 192.0.0/24) are not standard internal-service hosts, so the gap looks academic.

masking: T5 is masked by T1: while 'follow' lets fetch auto-follow redirects with no loopback check at all (index.ts:439 requires manual), the second fetch site's rebinding is not the live route; it becomes reachable only after T1 is fixed with a checked redirect loop.
T4's rebinding becomes decisive once T3 and T7 are fixed: after the resolver answer is fully validated the check still runs on the DNS answer, not on the peer actually connected at index.ts:430.

conflicts.what: Pinning the connection to the address returned by resolveDNSHost (T4 fix) conflicts with keeping 'follow' redirects working: one pinned lookup either breaks cross-host redirect hops or leaves them unresolved, while the T1 fix needs a per-hop check that preserves the documented 'follow' behaviour exercised at __tests__/index.spec.ts:258-275.

A natural T4 fix that rewrites the fetch target to the resolved IP also rewrites the URL returned as the preview url, which existing tests assert equals the input URL (__tests__/index.spec.ts:10, 26, 232); pinning must happen at the connection layer so the reported url stays intact.

Making resolveDNSHost mandatory (T2) forces every existing no-option call (__tests__/index.spec.ts:6, 24, 89) through a resolver the library does not have in browser/React Native runtimes, while the T3 classifier needs the same answer in a family-independent form.

Rejecting loopback for the URL actually fetched (T6) also rejects a localhost proxy, a documented proxyUrl use (__tests__/index.spec.ts:157-177), whereas T1 wants a loopback rule applied to redirect targets; a single rule cannot serve both without a proxy exemption.

fairness_risks: Requiring resolveDNSHost or adding a mandatory resolver contradicts README.md:100 and breaks callers that legitimately run in browsers/React Native where DNS resolution is unavailable; the library's own tests call getLinkPreview with no options (__tests__/index.spec.ts:6, 24, 89).

A blanket rule that any non-public resolved address is refused also refuses legitimate previews of intranet/self-hosted pages and localhost dev servers; the proxy option exists precisely to fetch through a trusted third party (__tests__/index.spec.ts:157-177).
Rejecting IPv6 answers wholesale, or every address containing a colon, breaks legitimate IPv6-only public sites; the rule has to classify addresses, not families.
Binding the check to the connected peer by rewriting the fetch URL breaks TLS/vhost correctness and the documented response url value that tests assert (__tests__/index.spec.ts:10, 26, 232).

Keeping followRedirects 'follow' working (README.md:98, __tests__/index.spec.ts:258-275) while checking every hop means reimplementing redirect following; a rule that simply refuses redirects breaks a documented, test-covered option.

The legitimate input shape that must keep working is a public hostname that resolves to a public address while redirects on the same hostname are followed (README.md:145-164); an over-broad same-host or reject-all-redirects rule is not acceptable.

design.why: Three independent judgements with three different dismissals: 'follow' is an opted-in mode so redirect hops need no check (T1), the resolver answer is normally an IPv4 quad so the blocklist looks complete (T3), and the library already resolves and rejects private answers so the connection looks guarded (T4). No single fix closes the others: T1 needs a checked manual redirect loop that preserves the documented 'follow' behaviour, T3 needs a family- and range-aware address classifier, T4 needs the checked answer bound to the connection actually made. T2 (no resolver means no check at all) is a fourth candidate with the strongest dismissal but the weakest hidden-test story, because making the hook mandatory contradicts README.md:100 and every no-option call; T5 shares T4's fix site (same group, and it is masked by T1), T6's wrong-object check sits on the trusted proxy path with no in-library SSRF consequence, and T7 is grouped with T3.
